title: Africa in One Level
objective: After this level you can describe Africa's size and how its landscapes change from north to south.
summary: Africa is the second-largest continent. The Equator cuts it almost in half, so its climates are mirrored: rainforest in the middle, then savanna, desert and Mediterranean tips.

cards.headline: Three famous lines of latitude cross Africa. No other continent gets all three.
cards.body: The Equator, the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn from Level 4 all run through it. That's a clue to how big Africa is, and to how its landscapes are laid out.

cards.headline: Bigger than your map admits
cards.body: Africa is the second-largest continent, after Asia, and covers about one-fifth of Earth's land. Your wall map probably undersells it. Remember Level 2: Africa is about 14 times bigger than Greenland, yet on a Mercator map they look like rivals. Mercator inflates places far from the Equator, and the Equator cuts Africa almost exactly in half. Greenland gets the boost. Africa doesn't.

cards.headline: A continent folded in half
cards.body: With the Equator through its middle, Africa's climates copy themselves on each side, like a folded inkblot. Wet rainforest sits in the center. Move north or south and it opens into savanna, grassland with scattered trees. Farther out come the deserts: the Sahara in the north, the Kalahari and the Namib in the south. At the far tips, north and south, you'll find Mediterranean climates.
cards.callout: Rainforest › savanna › desert › Mediterranean, in both directions

mascot.line: Fold Africa along the Equator and its climates nearly line up. Geography's neatest party trick.

cards.fact: Savanna covers almost half of Africa.
cards.context: So the safari picture of grass and scattered trees isn't a postcard cliché. It's the most typical Africa there is. The mirror isn't perfect, though: thanks to the bulge of western Africa, more of the continent lies north of the Equator than south of it.

cards.headline: Africa: sized up
learned: Mercator maps make it look smaller than it is
The Equator cuts it almost in half
Its climates mirror north and south: rainforest, savanna, desert

questions.prompt: Where does Africa rank among the continents by size?
questions.explanation: Africa is the second-largest continent, after Asia, with about one-fifth of Earth's land.

questions.prompt: Why do Africa's climate zones repeat in the same order north and south of its middle?

options.label: The Sahara spreads south every year
options.rationale: The Sahara stays in the north; the pattern comes from latitude.

options.label: Mountains split it into two equal halves
options.rationale: No mountain wall does it; a line of latitude does.

options.label: The Equator cuts it almost in half
Every coast has the same ocean current
options.rationale: Currents differ; the Equator sets the pattern.

questions.explanation: The Equator runs through Africa's middle, so climates change in the same order heading north or south: rainforest, savanna, desert, Mediterranean.

questions.prompt: From Level 4: which set of lines crosses Africa and no other continent?

options.label: The Equator and both polar circles
options.rationale: The polar circles are nowhere near Africa.

options.label: Only the Equator
options.rationale: Other continents cross the Equator too.

options.label: The two tropics and the Arctic Circle
options.rationale: The Arctic Circle is far to the north.

questions.explanation: Africa is the only continent crossed by the Equator, the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn.
